items.title: Identifying True Statements Regarding Extrema of Exponential Functions Over the Reals

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x) = -6\left(\dfrac12\right)^{x} - 4.] Which of the following statements are true?

  1. [MATH: f] has a minimum value.

  2. [MATH: f] does NOT have a maximum value.

  3. The range of [MATH: f] is [MATH: (-\infty,-4).]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x) = -6\left(\dfrac12\right)^{x} - 4.] Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: f] has a minimum value.
2. [MATH: f] does NOT have a maximum value.
3. The range of [MATH: f] is [MATH: (-\infty,-4).]

sections.normalized_html:
On the domain [MATH: x\in(-\infty,\infty),] an exponential function [MATH: f(x)=a\cdot b^x+c] approaches, but never reaches, a horizontal asymptote on one side, and increases (or decreases) without bound on the other.

Let's start by sketching the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] below.

From the graph, we note the following:

  • Looking at the end-behavior on the left-hand side, we see that [MATH: f(x) \to -\infty] as [MATH: x \to -\infty.]

  • Looking at the end-behavior on the right-hand side, we see that [MATH: f(x) < -4.]

With this in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is false. The function decreases without bound as [MATH: x\to -\infty,] so it does not have a minimum value.

  • Statement II is true. Since [MATH: f(x)] approaches the horizontal asymptote [MATH: y=-4] from below but never reaches [MATH: -4,] [MATH: f] does not have a maximum value.

  • Statement III is true. Since [MATH: f(x)] can be made arbitrarily negative and approaches [MATH: -4] from below, the range is [MATH: (-\infty,-4).]

Therefore, the correct statements are “II and III only”.
